body_markdown:
*Mark* writes:


I have a 1995 Buick Century sedan my parents purchased when it was just a few months old. (I know its service history.) A few weeks ago, I turned on the headlights. While the amber running lights went on, the headlights didn’t. Both headlights were off.


I took the Buick to a very competent shop. They checked the fuse and relay; no problems. They replaced the left headlight bulb. I saw both lights lit at the shop. Several days later—no headlights. Do you think it’s the switch? Or what else to check?


*Sajeev* answers:


Replacing only one[headlight bulb](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/drop-in-led-headlights-are-better-still-not-good-enough/) ? Because of the Buick’s age and the fact that headlight filaments are a wear item, I would be inclined to replace the other bulb. Maybe the Century doesn’t get driven at night? But this isn’t a problem we need to discuss, because we have another potential wear item on the menu: The Headlight Switch!


I’d be remiss if I didn’t tell you to get factory repair manual(s) for your car (or any GM A-body vehicle from this era). That said, telling someone to “go read a book” doesn’t necessarily make for good online storytelling.


There’s a higher-level check that doesn’t involve getting buried in a repair manual: Let’s first inspect the condition of the headlight connectors. Look for corrosion, loose wires, or even broken tabs on the headlight connector. Also check for voltage at the plug[using a multimeter](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/how-to-use-a-multimeter/) . It should be at or slightly over 12 volts. Do this for both the low and high beams.


Buick


Buick


Since both headlight bulbs are out, I’ll tempt fate and suggest the headlight switch is toast. If the fuse/relay are indeed good, it’s entirely possible that the switch has failed internally, or its connector went bad. Both the replacement headlight switch ($10 to $20) and its connector ($20) are cheap on Rock Auto. Because I do not have the aforementioned wiring diagrams, I will go out on a limb and suggest these headlight switches run 12-volt current from the battery like older GM designs, and that feed has cooked the switch. If so, there’s a good chance the connector is also toasted.


So remove whatever trim is covering the switch, unbolt the switch from the dashboard, disconnect the switch, and look at the connector’s pins for signs of an electrical malfunction. I wouldn’t be surprised if one pin looks melted and charred, and that one is responsible for taking battery juice and transferring it to the headlights.


This is all armchair quarterbacking, and you might not need a new headlight switch + connector. The problem might just be the switch, but I have a feeling they both failed. A few minutes with basic hand tools will tell you just how brown and melty it looks in there.
